screens.title: One rate for three years
screens.prose: Back to £100 growing to £113.40 over three years. The dashed line grows at the same rate every year and ends in the same place. That rate is the **annualised return**.
screens.question: What steady yearly rate turns £100 into £113.40 in three years?

hints.text: A steady rate $a$ for three years multiplies by $(1 + a)^3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the cube root of 1.134, then subtract 1.

byKey.divide: You divided 13.4% by 3. That ignores compounding: $1.0447^3 = 1.140$, too much.
byKey.average: That is the arithmetic average of the three returns. It overstates the steady rate.

explain.text: We need $(1 + a)^3 = 1.134$, so $a = 1.134^{1/3} - 1 = 4.28\%$. Over $T$ years the annualised return is $(1 + R)^{1/T} - 1$. It sits below the 5% average because the returns varied.

screens.title: Returns that add
screens.prose: The **log return** of a year is $\ln(1 + R)$. In the Series and Approximation course you saw it is close to $R - R^2/2$. The three years were +20%, −10% and +5%.
screens.question: Add the three log returns.

feedback.correct: 0.1258, which is $\ln 1.134$: log returns add up to the log of the total.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the natural log of each $1 + R$, then add.

byKey.simple: You added the simple returns. Take $\ln(1 + R)$ of each first.
byKey.pct: Give it as a decimal: 0.1258, not 12.58.

explain.text: $\ln 1.2 + \ln 0.9 + \ln 1.05 = \ln(1.2 \times 0.9 \times 1.05) = \ln 1.134 = 0.1258$. Logs turn the product of growth factors into a sum. So log returns add across time, and simple returns compound.

screens.title: The rules for returns
screens.prose:
Growth factors multiply: over $T$ years the total is $1 + R = (1 + R_1)(1 + R_2)\cdots(1 + R_T)$, and
$$\text{annualised} = (1 + R)^{1/T} - 1$$
Log returns, $\ln(1 + R_t)$, simply add.
screens.question: A strategy makes +80%, +60%, −100% and +200% in four years. What is its total return?

options.why: You added the returns. The −100% year multiplies the value by 0.
You averaged them. A factor of 0 makes the product 0, whatever else happens.
200% of nothing is nothing. Once the value is £0, no return brings it back.

feedback.correct: −100%. One factor of 0 makes the whole product 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the four growth factors.

explain.text: The factors are 1.8, 1.6, 0 and 3, and their product is 0. A return of −100% is total loss, and nothing compounds from zero. Its log return is $\ln 0$, minus infinity.

screens.title: Return for the risk
screens.prose: Cash in a bank earns the **risk-free rate**, here 4% a year. The **excess return** is what a fund earns above it. The **Sharpe ratio** divides that by the volatility, the standard deviation of yearly returns.
screens.question: What is Fund A's Sharpe ratio?

feedback.correct: 0.42: 5% of excess return for 12% of volatility.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the excess return by the volatility.

byKey.no-rf: You divided the whole 9% by the volatility. Subtract the 4% risk-free rate first.
byKey.excess: That is the excess return, 5%. Divide it by the 12% volatility.
byKey.inverse: You divided the volatility by the excess return. It is the other way up.

explain.text: $(0.09 - 0.04)/0.12 = 0.42$. It measures excess return per unit of risk. The Distributions and Limit Theorems course shows how long a record must be before a Sharpe ratio means anything.

formula.name: Annualised return
formula.note: $R$ is the total return over $T$ years. Never divide $R$ by $T$, or multiply a monthly return by 12.
